subject: botany_2
question_text: Give a brief account of Bt cotton.

mark_split.label: How the toxin kills the insect

insider_note: The mechanism is where the marks are: protoxin, alkaline gut, activation, pores, lysis. Write those five words in order and the third mark is safe.

steps.label: What Bt cotton is
steps.margin_note: Definition, the bacterium in full, and the three insect groups.
lines: BT COTTON is a genetically modified (GM) cotton
variety that makes its own INSECTICIDAL
PROTEIN, which kills the cotton bollworm.
It was created using genes from the bacterium
BACILLUS THURINGIENSIS — Bt for short.
The bacterium's proteins kill certain insects:
lepidopterans (tobacco budworm), coleopterans
(beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).
steps.why: The plant makes the insecticide itself, so the toxin is present in every cell and cannot be washed off or rained away.
common_mistakes: Saying Bt cotton is sprayed with an insecticide. The plant MAKES the insecticidal protein itself.
Expanding Bt wrongly. It is Bacillus thuringiensis.
steps.memory_tip: Bt is the bacterium; the cotton carries its gene.

steps.label: The Bt toxin crystal
steps.margin_note: The crystal, the protoxin, and why the bacterium is safe.
lines: Bacillus thuringiensis forms PROTEIN CRYSTALS
during a particular phase of its growth.
These crystals contain a toxic INSECTICIDAL
PROTEIN.
The toxin exists in the crystal as an INACTIVE
PROTOXIN.
The bacterium itself is not killed by it,
because the toxin is inactive while stored.
steps.why: Storing the toxin in an inactive form is how the bacterium avoids poisoning itself, and it is also why the toxin is harmless until eaten.
common_mistakes: Saying the crystal is active toxin. It is an INACTIVE PROTOXIN.
Not saying why the bacterium survives. The inactive form is the reason.
steps.memory_tip: Stored inactive, so it harms nothing until it is eaten.

steps.label: How the toxin kills the insect
steps.margin_note: Six numbered steps. The alkaline pH is the step examiners look for.
lines: 1. The insect EATS the inactive protoxin.
2. The ALKALINE pH of the insect gut dissolves
the crystals.
3. The protoxin is converted into the ACTIVE
form of the toxin.
4. The active toxin binds to the surface of the
MIDGUT EPITHELIAL cells.
5. It creates PORES in those cells, so they
swell and burst (LYSE).
6. The insect dies.
steps.why: Human and most animal stomachs are acidic, so the protoxin is never activated in them — which is the whole basis of the claim that Bt crops are safe to eat.
common_mistakes: Saying the toxin is active when eaten. It is activated by the insect's ALKALINE gut.
Leaving out the alkaline pH. It is what makes the toxin specific to insects.
Saying it kills by poisoning the blood. It makes PORES in the midgut cells.
steps.memory_tip: Alkaline gut switches it on; acid stomachs do not.

steps.label: The cry genes
steps.margin_note: Both gene sets with their pests, and the specificity point.

lines.text: Cry I Ac and Cry II Ab for bollworm;
Cry I Ab for corn borer

lines: The toxin is coded by genes named CRY.
Most Bt toxins are INSECT GROUP SPECIFIC, so a
different cry gene is needed for each pest.
The proteins of CRY I Ac and CRY II Ab control
the cotton bollworms.
The protein of CRY I Ab controls the CORN BORER.
Specific cry genes were isolated from Bacillus
thuringiensis and put into crop plants.
steps.why: Each cry protein binds only to receptors present in certain insect guts, which is why the gene has to be matched to the pest.
common_mistakes: Swapping the genes. Cry I Ac and Cry II Ab are for BOLLWORM; Cry I Ab is for CORN BORER.
Saying one cry gene works on all pests. They are insect group SPECIFIC.
steps.memory_tip: Cotton takes Cry I Ac and Cry II Ab; the corn borer takes Cry I Ab — the roman numeral separates the two Ab genes.
